notes.text: Because thou art my brother — That is, kinsman. Should thou therefore serve me for nought? - No, what reason for that? If Jacob be so respectful as to give him his service without demanding any consideration for it, yet Laban will not be so unjust as to take advantage either of his necessity, or of his good nature. It appears by computation that Jacob was now seventy years old when he bound himself apprentice for a wife; probably Rachel was young and scarce marriageable when Jacob came first, which made him the more willing to stay for her till his seven years were expired.
They seemed to him but a few days for the love he had to her — An age of work will be but as a few days to those that love God, and long for Christ's appearing.
Behold it was Leah — Jacob had cheated his own father when he pretended to be Esau, and now his father-in-law cheated him. Herein, how unrighteous soever Laban was, the Lord was righteous.

It must be so done in our country — We have reason to think there was no such custom in his country; but if there was, and that he resolved to observe it, he should have told Jacob so, when he undertook to serve him for his younger daughter.

We will give thee this also — Hereby he drew Jacob into the sin and snare, and disquiet of multiplying wives. Jacob did not design it, but to have kept as true to Rachel as his father had done to Rebekah; he that had lived without a wife to the eighty fourth year of his age could then have been very well content with one: but Laban to dispose of his two daughters without portions, and to get seven years service more out of Jacob, thus imposeth upon him, and draws him into such a strait, that he had some colourable reason for marrying them both.

glossa.text: « He kissed her. » ((AUG.)) It was the custom, chiefly in that simplicity of the ancients, that kinsfolk should kiss kinsfolk, and it is done today in many places. But it may be asked: how did she receive a kiss from one unknown, if Jacob afterwards declared the kinship? It is therefore to be understood: either that he, who knew the kinship, confidently rushed to a kiss, or that Scripture afterwards narrated it by recapitulation, since Jacob first declared who he was.

« The name of the elder was Lia, » etc. Victorinus the martyr interpreted Rachel and Lia into the likeness of the Church and the Synagogue. He judges that Lia, the elder by birth, signifies the Synagogue, because she first bore the people of God: who is said to be blear-eyed, because the law given through Moses was wrought together and sealed. Rachel, the younger and the fair, first barren, afterwards fruitful, signifies the Church, which is later in time, but holy in body and in spirit. Her eyes are comely, because they deserved to see the Gospel. But she was long barren while the Synagogue brought forth a people. Jacob served for Rachel, and Lia is put under him in her stead: because Christ, that he might take the Church to himself, first joined the Synagogue to himself.

« Jacob therefore served seven years for Rachel. » The servitude of Jacob of seven years for two wives signifies the time of the present life, which is rolled round in seven days; in which the Lord took the form of a servant, obedient to the Father unto death. Jacob served, because « the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister ((Matth. XX)): » He fed sheep, and Christ said ((Joan. X)): « I am the good shepherd. » He took to himself for a reward the party-coloured flock: Christ gathered to himself the variety of divers nations. He set three rods, the barks being stripped off, in the troughs of the waters, that by the beholding of them the sheep might be multiplied: and our Lord set before the faithful people, in the water of baptism, the names of the three persons, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, that he who shall have looked upon this with a full heart may be made a sheep of God.

« And they seemed to him but a few days, » etc. It is to be asked: how was this said, since even a short time seems long to them that love? It was said therefore because of the labour of the servitude, which love made easy.

((AUG., lib. XXII contra Faustum.)) Four wives are cast up against Jacob as a huge crime. But since it was then the custom, it was not a crime; now however it is a crime, because it is not the custom, etc., *as far as* save the burning of carnal concupiscence.

((ISID., in Gen., tom. V.)) There are therefore two free wives of Jacob, for both are daughters of the remission of sins, etc., *as far as* and he saw in the beginning the Word with God, and wills to bring forth, and cannot, because « who shall declare his generation? » ((Act. VIII.))

((ISID.)) Two free wives of Jacob, because two lives are preached to us in the body of Jesus Christ, etc., *as far as* But this cannot be in the land of the dying, which is signified by these words.

« It is not the custom in our place, » etc. ((ID., ibid.)) She is called the elder who is the earlier in time, etc., *as far as* to one thing therefore we must tend, but for this many things must be borne.

((ID., ibid.)) Accordingly the life which suits the study of contemplation, etc., *as far as* whence below in XXX: « Rachel was jealous of her sister. »

((ID., ibid.)) Accordingly, because a pure understanding of that divine substance, etc., *as far as* not because a divine power.

notes.text: Glory — Glory in the God whom you serve, as the only true God.
Seek — The Lord in his strength, in his sanctuary, or before the ark, which is called God's strength. Face - His gracious presence.
Judgments — The punishments which he brought upon Egypt by his mere word.
Of Jacob — The only branch of Abraham's seed to whom the following blessings belong.
Judgments — God executes his judgments upon all nations and people.
Remembered — So as to perform it. The word - The promise. Commanded - Established. Thousand generations - To all generations.
Oath — Wherewith he ratified the covenant with Isaac, Gen. xxvi, 3.
A law — That it might be as firm and irrevocable as a law.
Lot — The portion assigned to you by lot.

glossa.text:
*Alleluia.* ((CASS.)) Here for the first time *alleluia,* nor was it set down before this by anyone; and no tongue has presumed to change it. *Alleluia,* praise ye. *Ia* is the name of the invisible God, which belongs to him alone. Through twenty psalms, which have this title, the great works of God are told, and great is the exultation in them. ((CASS.)) Here the prophet commends the good among that people of Israel, who together with other believers are the true seed of Abraham, the children of the promise.

*Give glory to the Lord.* ((AUG.)) The first psalm to which alleluia is prefixed, etc., *as far as* he subjoins what temporal things the mercy of God gave them.
*All things:* ((CASS.)) all things; there is nothing that shame should keep silent. Or, all the things which they shall tell are wonderful, for no one can relate them all.

*Be ye praised in the name,* that is, rejoice that you are called Christians from Christ.

((AUG.)) Be ye praised: he does not forbid being praised, if they are good; if they are not, then not save in the Lord, who makes men good. Be ye praised in the name. Which elsewhere is, *In the Lord shall my soul be praised:* what he adds there, *let the meek hear and rejoice:* here too in a manner, *let the heart rejoice,* as if he should say,

*The face,* etc. ((ID.)) That is, the presence, etc., *as far as* the wicked man can fear the presence which the good man loves. ((HIER.)) From the martyr Hippolytus, etc., *as far as* there about to take his Church from among the Gentiles.

*Remember, and the rest.* ((AUG.)) Seek him, etc., *as far as* if it is a great thing to seek what God is, at least behold the things which he has made. *The wonders,* etc. ((ID.)) Little by little he ascends from visible wonders to judgments: thence to the everlasting testament, where there is both precept and promise.

*In all the earth.* ((ID.)) Think not that the sons of Abraham are in one nation according to the flesh, because in all the earth are Jacob and Israel, to whom he makes known his judgments, but not to another nation.

*For ever,* ((ID.)) that is, unto eternity, whence afterwards, unto an everlasting testament. Which testament, if it be taken as the Old on account of the land of Chanaan, of which it follows. How is it everlasting, since that earthly inheritance cannot be everlasting? *Of the testament.* For that is called a testament which is promised, and the teaching in which the promise is declared, and for the keeping of which it is rendered. ((ID.)) The promise is what we ought to receive: the commandment, what we ought to do. This is faith, that the just man live by faith, and to this faith an inheritance *haere ditas* is promised. *Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.* Behold three patriarchs, whose God he calls himself in a special manner: *I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob.* Behold a threefold authority.
*Unto an everlasting testament,* ((ID.)) that is, that from the very word fulfilled, etc., *as far as* and the son abides in the house for ever.

*The land of Chanaan,* ((CASS.)) that is, that which is signified by it: for he gave this land also as a figure of the eternal inheritance ((I Joan. IV)). ((AUG.)) Fittingly the eternal inheritance is called the land of Chanaan, because from it servants are driven off and sons received.

notes.text: Likewise the Spirit — Nay, not only the universe, not only the children of God, but the Spirit of God also himself, as it were, groaneth, while he helpeth our infirmities, or weaknesses. Our understandings are weak, particularly in the things of God our desires are weak; our prayers are weak. We know not - Many times. What we should pray for - Much less are we able to pray for it as we ought: but the Spirit maketh intercession for us - In our hearts, even as Christ does in heaven. With groanings - The matter of which is from ourselves, but the Spirit forms them; and they are frequently inexpressible, even by the faithful themselves.

But he who searcheth the hearts — Wherein the Spirit dwells and intercedes. Knoweth - Though man cannot utter it. What is the mind of the Spirit, for he maketh intercession for the saints - Who are near to God. According to God - According to his will, as is worthy of God. and acceptable to him.

And we know — This in general; though we do not always know particularly what to pray for. That all things - Ease or pain, poverty or riches, and the ten thousand changes of life. Work together for good - Strongly and sweetly for spiritual and eternal good. To them that are called according to his purpose - His gracious design of saving a lost world by the death of his Son. This is a new proposition. St. Paul, being about to recapitulate the whole blessing contained in justification, (termed "glorification," ver. 30,) first goes back to the purpose or decree of God, which is frequently mentioned in holy writ. To explain this (nearly in the words of an eminent writer) a little more at large:-When a man has a work of time and importance before him, he pauses, consults, and contrives; and when he has laid a plan, resolves or decrees to proceed accordingly. Having observed this in ourselves, we are ready to apply it to God also; and he, in condescension to us has applied it to himself. The works of providence and redemption are vast and stupendous, and therefore we are apt to conceive of God as deliberating and consulting on them, and then decreeing to act according to "the counsel of his own will;" as if, long before the world was made, he had been concerting measures both as to the making and governing of it, and had then writ down his decrees, which altered not, any more than the laws of the Medes and Persians. Whereas, to take this consulting and decreeing in a literal sense, would be the same absurdity as to ascribe a real human body and human passions to the ever-blessed God. This is only a popular representation of his infallible knowledge and unchangeable wisdom; that is, he does all things as wisely as a man can possibly do, after the deepest consultation, and as steadily pursues the most proper method as one can do who has laid a scheme beforehand. But then, though the effects be such as would argue consultation and consequent decrees in man, yet what need of a moment's consultation in Him who sees all things at one view? Nor had God any more occasion to pause and deliberate, and lay down rules for his own conduct from all eternity, than he has now. What was there any fear of his mistaking afterwards, if he had not beforehand prepared decrees, to direct him what he was to do? Will any man say, he was wiser before the creation than since? or had he then more leisure, that he should take that opportunity to settle his affairs, and make rules (or himself, from which he was never to vary? He has doubtless the same wisdom and all other perfections at this day which he had from eternity; and is now as capable of making decrees, or rather has no more occasion for them now than formerly: his understanding being always equally clear and bright, his wisdom equally infallible.

Whom he foreknew, he also predestinated conformable to the image of his Son — Here the apostle declares who those are whom he foreknew and predestinated to glory; namely, those who are conformable to the image of his Son. This is the mark of those who are foreknown and will be glorified, 2 Tim. ii, 19. Phil. iii, 10, 21.

Them he — In due time. Called - By his gospel and his Spirit. And whom he called - When obedient to the heavenly calling, Acts xxvi, 19. He also justified - Forgave and accepted. And whom he justified - Provided they "continued in his goodness," chap. xi, 22, he in the end glorified - St. Paul does not affirm, either here or in any other part of his writings, that precisely the same number of men are called, justified, and glorified. He does not deny that a believer may fall away and be cut off between his special calling and his glorification, chap. xi, 22. Neither does he deny that many are called who never are justified. He only affirms that this is the method whereby God leads us step by step toward heaven. He glorified - He speaks as one looking back from the goal, upon the race of faith. Indeed grace, as it is glory begun, is both an earnest and a foretaste of eternal glory.

What shall we say then to these things — Related in the third, fifth, and eighth chapters? As if he had said, We cannot go, think, or wish anything farther. If God be for us - Here follow four periods, one general and three particular. Each begins with glorying in the grace of God, which is followed by a question suitable to it, challenging all opponents to all which, "I am persuaded," &c., is a general answer. The general period is, If God be for us, who can be against us? The first particular period, relating to the past time, is, He that spared not his own Son, how shall he not freely give us all things? The second, relating to the present, is, It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? The third, relating to the future, is, It is Christ that died - Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?

He that — This period contains four sentences: He spared not his own Son; therefore he will freely give us all things. He delivered him up for us all; therefore, none can lay anything to our charge. Freely - For all that follows justification is a free gift also. All things - Needful or profitable for us.

God's elect — The above-cited author observes, that long before the coming of Christ the heathen world revolted from the true God, and were therefore reprobated, or rejected. But the nation of the Jews were chosen to be the people of God, and were therefore styled, "the children" or "sons of God," Deut. xiv, 1; "holy people," Deut. vii, 6; xiv, 2; "a chosen seed," Deut. iv, 37; "the elect," Isaiah xli, 8, 9; xliii, 10; "the called of God," Isaiah xlviii, 12. And these titles were given to all the nation of Israel, including both good and bad. Now the gospel having the most strict connection with the Books of the Old Testament, where these phrases frequently occur; and our Lord and his apostles being native Jews, and beginning to preach in the land of Israel, the language in which they preached would of course abound with the phrases of the Jewish nation. And hence it is easy to see why such of them as would not receive him were styled reprobated. For they no longer continued to be the people of God; whereas this and those other honourable titles were continued to all such Jews as embraced Christianity. And the same appellations which once belonged to the Jewish nation were now given to the gentile Christians also together with which they were invested with all the privileges of "the chosen people of God;" and nothing could cut them off from these but their own wilful apostasy. It does not appear that even good men were ever termed God's elect till above two thousand years from the creation. God's electing or choosing the nation of Israel, and separating them from the other nations, who were sunk in idolatry and all wickedness, gave the first occasion to this sort of language. And as the separating the Christians from the Jews was a like event, no wonder it was expressed in like words and phrases only with this difference, the term elect was of old applied to all the members of the visible church; whereas in the New Testament it is applied only to the members of the invisible.

Yea rather, that is risen — Our faith should not stop at his death, but be exercised farther on his resurrection, kingdom, second coming. Who maketh intercession for us - Presenting there his obedience, his sufferings, his prayers, and our prayers sanctified through him.

Who shall separate us from the love of Christ — Toward us? Shall affliction or distress - He proceeds in order, from less troubles to greater: can any of these separate us from his protection in it; and, if he sees good, deliverance from it?
All the day — That is, every day, continually. We are accounted - By our enemies; by ourselves. Psalm xliv, 22.
We more than conquer — We are not only no losers, but abundant gainers, by all these trials. This period seems to describe the full assurance of hope.

I am persuaded — This is inferred from the thirty-fourth verse, in an admirable order: - Neither death" shall hurt us; For "Christ is dead:" "Nor life;" 'is risen" Nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers; nor things pre- sent, nor things to come;" "is at the right hand of God:" "Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature;" "maketh intercession for us." Neither death - Terrible as it is to natural men; a violent death in particular, ver. 36. Nor life - With all the affliction and distress it can bring, ver. 35; or a long, easy life; or all living men. Nor angels - Whether good (if it were possible they should attempt it) or bad, with all their wisdom and strength. Nor principalities, nor powers - Not even those of the highest rank, or the most eminent power. Nor things present - Which may befall us during our pilgrimage; or the whole world, till it passeth away. Nor things to come - Which may occur either when our time on earth is past, or when time itself is at an end, as the final judgment, the general conflagration, the everlasting fire. Nor height, nor depth - The former sentence respected the differences of times; this, the differences of places. How many great and various things are contained in these words, we do not, need not, cannot know yet. The height - In St. Paul's sublime style, is put for heaven. The depth - For the great abyss: that is, neither the heights, I will not say of walls, mountains, seas, but, of heaven itself, can move us; nor the abyss itself, the very thought of which might astonish the boldest creature. Nor any creature - Nothing beneath the Almighty; visible enemies he does not even deign to name. Shall be able - Either by force, ver. 35; or by any legal claim, ver. 33, &c. To separate us from the love of God in Christ - Which will surely save, protect, deliver us who believe in, and through, and from, them all. In this chapter St. Paul, after strongly declaring his love and esteem for them, sets himself to answer the grand objection of his countrymen; namely, that the rejection of the Jews and reception of the gentiles was contrary to the word of God. That he had not here the least thought of personal election or reprobation is manifest,

glossa.text:
*Unutterable.* For how should that be uttered which is desired, when it is unknown? Yet it is not altogether unknown. For if it were utterly unknown, it would not be desired. And again, if it were seen, it would not be sought with groanings.

*He searcheth. ((AMBR.))* Not as though seeking what he knows not, to whom nothing is hidden, and to whom the prayer of all spirits is known.

*But we know that to them that love,* etc. As if he should say: Not only does the Holy Spirit do this, but he also makes all things turn out unto good for them that love him, whether prosperous or adverse; for such a God comforts by prosperous things, exercises by adverse. Profitable therefore are the evils which the faithful piously endure, either for the amending or the taking away of sins, or for the exercising and proving of justice, or for the showing forth of the misery of this life. For although the death of the flesh came originally from the sin of the first man, yet the good use of it has made most glorious martyrs. And therefore not only it, but all the evils of the world also, had to remain when sins were remitted, that man might have wherewith to contend for the truth, and whence the virtue of the faithful might be exercised.

*According to the purpose.* As if he should say: That they are called is from nothing else than from the predestination of God. And thence it is that *all things work together unto good:* not from merit.

*For whom,* God, *he predestinated,* that is, prepared by grace bestowed that they should believe the word of preaching: those *he foreknew,* that is, long before knew beforehand, *to be made conformable to the Son,* who is the image of the Father, in every way the same with the Father. Whence it is said: *He that seeth me seeth the Father also ((Joan. XIV))*.

*Of the image.* That we may bear the image of the heavenly, as we have borne the image of the earthly. Or *the firstborn.* Because before every creature he was not made but born, and because he was the first born without sin, and the first to rise again impassible, in which he has brethren.

*He called.* The outward calling is made through preachers and is common to the good and to the bad. But the inward is of the elect only. Of the outward it is said: *Many are called, but few chosen.* By calling predestination is fulfilled. To call is to help the knowledge concerning faith, or to prick him whom he makes to hear, and this is of the elect only. *He magnified.* This of the foreknown, not of the others, who, although they believe for a time and seem good, yet because they do not abide, are not magnified. *He magnified,* or *he shall magnify:* but this is to come, and yet it is spoken as past: because God is said to have done the things which from eternity he disposed to do; whence Isaias: *Who hath made the things that are to come ((Isa. XLIV))*. To such all things are unto good, even that they go astray, that thereby they may be the more wary, and not trusting in themselves. Four things are here mentioned: predestination, calling, justification, magnification. One is in God, and three in us. For our predestination is not in us, but hidden with him in his foreknowledge. But the three remaining are in us.

*If God be for us. ((AUG.))* God is for us, that he should predestinate us before we were, that he should call us when we were turned away, that he should justify us when we were sinners, and glorify us when we were mortal.

*He delivered up.* This is said because the Father delivered up the Son; but the author of this cup is also he himself who drinks it. Whence the Apostle: *Christ loved us, and delivered himself up for us ((Ephes. V))*. If therefore the Father delivered up the Son, and the Son himself, what did Judas do? The Father in delivering up the Son did well; the Son in delivering up himself did well; Judas in delivering up his master for avarice did ill. For that which has been bestowed upon us out of the passion of Christ shall not be reckoned to the malice of Judas; he shall have the wage of malice, Christ the praise of grace. *All things.* It is less to give us all things than for our sake to deliver Christ up to death. And so all the higher things, namely God the Trinity, are ours for the seeing and the enjoying. Things equal, namely the angels, to whom we shall be made equal in the time to come, for the living together; but now we are inferior. Things lower also are ours for the ruling. And likewise certain higher things too, as the sublime angels and all the heavenly ministries of God, are ours, not by dominion, but by use; as the things of a lord are the servants', for sustenance, namely, or ornament, or aught else of this kind.

*At the right hand of God.* In the honour wherein he is God, whose petition cannot be contemned. *He maketh intercession.* While daily he offers to the Father's countenance the man whom he assumed, and the grievous kind of death which he bore for us.
*Who shall separate us,* etc. ((CYPR.)) None of these things can separate believers, etc., *as far as* that we also may suffer for his sake: *But in all these things we overcome.*
*Neither angels, nor princes, nor virtues.* These orders are taken of the evil angels, and of the good if it might be done.

*Neither height, nor depth.* That is, neither prosperity nor adversity, whence Solomon: *Riches and poverty give me not: lest, being filled, I become a liar, or, being poor, I rob, and forswear the name of God ((Prov. XXX))*. Many sin through height, many through need. Against this Ahaz is set forth in Isaias, who would not ask a sign either in the height or in the depth. The remedy is from Christ, who was neither lifted up by the power whereby he is equal to the Father, nor troubled at the casting out of death, who is a sign in the height and in the depth: lest he should either be exalted by royal power, or troubled by hardship, as it then was on account of the war of the Assyrians.

notes.text: He proposed to them another parable — The former parables relate chiefly to unfruitful hearers; these that follow, to those who bear good fruit. The kingdom of heaven - Both the Gospel dispensation, and the inward kingdom. Mark iv, 30; Luke xiii, 18.

The least — That is, one of the least: a way of speaking extremely common among the Jews. It becometh a tree - In those countries it grows exceeding large and high. So will the Christian doctrine spread in the world, and the life of Christ in the soul.
Three measures — This was the quantity which they usually baked at once: till the whole was leavened - Thus will the Gospel leaven the world and grace the Christian. Luke xiii, 20.

glossa.text: *The kingdom is like,* etc. The kingdom of heaven is the preaching of the Gospel, concerning which elsewhere: *The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you, and shall be given to a nation bringing forth the fruit thereof ((Matth. XXI))*. Or the knowledge of the Scriptures. *To a grain of mustard seed.* It is compared to a grain of mustard seed for the fervour of faith, because it is said to drive out poisons, that is, all the doctrines of depravity. In the grain of mustard seed the humility of the Lord's incarnation may be understood. Which being received, a man put it in his garden, because Joseph, receiving the body of the crucified Saviour, buried it in a garden. It spread out branches in which the birds of the air shall rest, because he scattered preachers throughout the world, in whose words and consolations the faithful might take breath from the weariness of this life.

*But when it is grown up.* In the whole world, or in the mind of each: because no one is perfect on a sudden. It grew and became a tree, because he rose again and ascended into heaven. Or it shall have grown, that is, it shall have become known to the minds of men how great its power is. The rest appear as herbs, which grow quickly and fall: not living, but withered: that becomes not an herb, but a tree, where there are leaves with fruit, and in its diverse meanings spiritual men rest.

*Than herbs, and becometh a tree.* That is, than the doctrines of the philosophers, which grow quickly and fall, promising nothing that has life.

*In three measures of meal.* That spirit, soul and body, brought into one, may not disagree among themselves. Or the three powers of the soul are brought into one, that in reason we may possess prudence, in anger the hatred of vices, in desire the longing for virtues. Or, the woman, the Church, mixes the faith of men in three measures of meal, in the belief of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. And when it has been leavened into one, it leads us not to a threefold God, but to the knowledge of one deity, because the nature is not diverse in the several persons.

*Until it was leavened.* So long ought charity, hidden in the mind, to grow, until it change the whole mind into its own perfection, so that it love or think upon nothing beside God, which is begun here, and perfected in the other life.

echoes.text: To Adam he said, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life. It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field. By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, […]
echoes.note: 'The creation was subjected to vanity... in hope' (vv.20-22) directly invokes the curse on the ground 'because of you,' the toil, thorns, and frustrated labor of the fall; creation's bondage to decay is the Edenic curse awaiting reversal.

echoes.text: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.
echoes.note: 'I create new heavens and a new earth' is the hope toward which the groaning creation strains (vv.19-22): the liberation of creation 'into the liberty of the glory of the children of God' is the prophetic new-creation renewal of the cosmos.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: Being 'conformed to the image of his Son' (v.29) reworks humanity's creation in the image of God; the restored image is now christological, the Son as the prototype to which the predestined are refashioned.

echoes.text: I will also appoint him my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.
echoes.note: 'I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth' grounds 'that he might be the firstborn among many brothers' (v.29); the Davidic-messianic firstborn title is extended to the Son who heads a redeemed family.

echoes.text: “Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher; “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.”
echoes.note: Creation 'subjected to vanity' (mataiotes, v.20) reuses the Septuagint's rendering of hevel ('vanity of vanities'); Qoheleth's diagnosis of the cosmos's futile, breath-like emptiness is the condition from which creation longs for release.

echoes.text: The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the young goat; The calf, the young lion, and the fattened calf together; and a little child will lead them. The cow and the bear will graze. Their young ones will lie down together. The lion will eat straw like the ox. The nursing child will play near a cobra’s hole, and the weaned child will put his hand on the viper’s den. They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain; for […]
echoes.note: The peaceable, restored creation under the messianic shoot — wolf with lamb, no harm in all God's holy mountain — anticipates creation 'delivered from the bondage of decay,' the redeemed cosmos liberated alongside God's children (vv.19-21).

echoes.text: Like as a woman with child, who draws near the time of her delivery, is in pain and cries out in her pangs; so we have been before you, Yahweh. We have been with child. We have been in pain. We gave birth, it seems, only to wind. We have not worked any deliverance in the earth; neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen.
echoes.note: 'Like a woman with child... we writhed in pain' supplies the birth-pang imagery of 'the whole creation groans and travails in pain together' (v.22); creation labors toward the deliverance of new life.

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
echoes.note: 'The LORD looks on the heart' undergirds 'he who searches the hearts knows what is on the Spirit's mind' (v.27); God's heart-discerning gaze validates the wordless intercession.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD search the heart and test the mind' supplies the precise epithet 'he who searches the hearts' (v.27); the heart-searcher reads the Spirit's unutterable groanings.

echoes.text: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn,
echoes.note: 'Israel is my firstborn son' reinforces the 'firstborn among many brothers' (v.29): the firstborn-son status, once Israel's, belongs to the Son who incorporates many siblings.

echoes.text: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
echoes.note: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you... I appointed you' supplies the foreknowing-and-appointing pattern of vv.29-30; divine foreknowledge as elective purpose precedes calling.

echoes.text: The earth mourns and fades away. The world languishes and fades away. The lofty people of the earth languish. The earth also is polluted under its inhabitants, because they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, and broken the everlasting covenant. Therefore the curse has devoured the earth, and those who dwell therein are found guilty. Therefore the inhabitants of the earth are burned, and few men left. The new wine mourns. The vine […]
echoes.note: 'The earth mourns and withers... the earth is defiled under its inhabitants' depicts the groaning land suffering under human transgression, parallel to creation subjected to futility and groaning (vv.20-22).

echoes.text: “Before she travailed, she gave birth; before her pain came, she delivered a son. Who has heard such a thing? who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? shall a nation be born at once? for as soon as Zion travailed, she gave birth to her children. Shall I bring to the birth, and not cause to be delivered?” says Yahweh: “shall I who cause to give birth shut the womb?” says your God.
echoes.note: Zion's travail bringing forth her children before her pain comes echoes the link between creation's birth-pangs (v.22) and the 'revealing of the children of God' / 'redemption of the body' (vv.19,23).

echoes.text: The sorrows of a travailing woman will come on him. He is an unwise son; for when it is time, he doesn’t come to the opening of the womb.
echoes.note: 'The pangs of childbirth come for him' as an image of judgment and impending deliverance resonates faintly with the cosmic travail of v.22.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
echoes.note: 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh' as eschatological down-payment resonates with 'the first fruits of the Spirit' (v.23), the Spirit as the firstfruits/guarantee of the coming redemption.

echoes.text: The first of the first fruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of Yahweh your God. “You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.
echoes.note: 'The first fruits of the Spirit' (v.23) draws on the cultic firstfruits offering that consecrates and pledges the full harvest; the Spirit is the consecrating pledge of the redeemed body.

echoes.text: Wake up! Why do you sleep, Lord? Arise! Don’t reject us forever. Why do you hide your face, and forget our affliction and our oppression? For our soul is bowed down to the dust. Our body clings to the earth. Rise up to help us. Redeem us for your loving kindness’ sake.
echoes.note: The lament's 'why do you sleep?... our soul is bowed down... redeem us' anticipates the groaning, waiting, and hoped-for redemption (vv.23-25); the same psalm is quoted at v.36.

echoes.text: Lord, all my desire is before you. My groaning is not hidden from you.
echoes.note: 'All my longing is before you; my groaning is not hidden from you' resonates with the inarticulate groaning the Spirit voices before 'him who searches the hearts' (vv.26-27).

echoes.text: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar.
echoes.note: 'O LORD, you have searched me and known me... you discern my thoughts from afar' resonates with God searching the hearts and knowing the Spirit's mind (v.27).

echoes.text: Listen, islands, to me; and listen, you peoples, from far: Yahweh has called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother has he made mention of my name:
echoes.note: The Servant 'called from the womb,' named before birth, resonates with the chain of foreknowing, predestining, and calling in vv.29-30.

echoes.text: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save many people alive.
echoes.note: 'You meant evil... but God meant it for good' faintly underlies 'all things work together for good for those who love God' (v.28); divine providence turning suffering toward good.

echoes.text: and showing loving kindness to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.
echoes.note: 'Showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments' supplies the covenantal designation 'those who love God' (v.28), the loving-God-and-being-blessed pattern.

echoes.text: Yes, for your sake we are killed all day long. We are regarded as sheep for the slaughter.
echoes.note: v.36 cites verbatim with the formula 'even as it is written': 'For your sake we are killed all day long; we were accounted as sheep for the slaughter.' The lament psalm of the righteous suffering for God's sake interprets the believers' affliction (v.35).

echoes.text: He is near who justifies me; who will bring charges against me? Let us stand up together: who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord Yahweh will help me; who is he who shall condemn me? Behold, all they shall wax old as a garment, the moth shall eat them up.
echoes.note: The Servant's courtroom taunt 'He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me?... It is the Lord GOD who helps me; who will declare me guilty?' is reworked into 'Who could bring a charge against God's chosen ones? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns?' (vv.33-34); the forensic question-and-answer pattern is shared.

echoes.text: He said, “Don’t lay your hand on the boy, neither do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.”
echoes.note: 'He who didn't spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all' (v.32) echoes the Aqedah, where God says to Abraham 'you have not withheld (spared) your son, your only son'; God now does for all what Abraham was prepared to do, the Father not sparing his own Son.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: 'Sit at my right hand' grounds 'who is at the right hand of God' (v.34); the enthronement of the exalted Lord secures his advocacy and the impossibility of any condemnation.

echoes.text: and said, “I have sworn by myself, says Yahweh, because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only son,
echoes.note: 'Because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son' reinforces v.32; the Septuagint's verb for 'spare/withhold' (pheidomai) is the same word Paul uses, strengthening the Aqedah allusion.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all' and the Servant 'delivered up' (LXX paradidomi, 53:6,12) stands behind 'delivered him up for us all' (v.32); the handing-over of the Servant for the many.

echoes.text: Yahweh is on my side. I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?
echoes.note: 'The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?' supplies the rhetorical shape of 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' (v.31); the same God-for-me-therefore-fearless logic.

echoes.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; And their departure was accounted to be their hurt, And their journeying away from us to be their ruin: But they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality; And having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; Because God made trial of them, and […]
echoes.note: 'The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them... having been disciplined a little they will receive great good' parallels the assurance that no affliction separates from God's love (vv.35-39); the righteous tested 'like gold in the furnace' and found worthy.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: The Servant 'poured out his soul to death... bore the sin of many and makes intercession for the transgressors' resonates with Christ who 'makes intercession for us' (v.34); both join self-giving death with ongoing intercession.

echoes.text: Only don’t rebel against Yahweh, neither fear the people of the land; for they are bread for us. Their defense is removed from over them, and Yahweh is with us. Don’t fear them.”
echoes.note: 'The LORD is with us; do not fear them' resonates with 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' (v.31); divine presence nullifies opposing power.

echoes.text: Then my enemies shall turn back in the day that I call. I know this, that God is for me.
echoes.note: 'This I know, that God is for me' is a near-verbal antecedent to 'God is for us' (v.31), the confidence that God's siding with the petitioner routs adversaries.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers came at me to eat up my flesh, even my adversaries and my foes, they stumbled and fell. Though an army should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear. Though war should rise against me, even then I will be confident.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?... though war arise against me, yet I will be confident' resonates with the catalogue of perils that cannot prevail (vv.35,37-39).

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'There is no god besides me... I kill and I make alive' underlies the totalizing pairing 'neither death, nor life' (v.38) as the extremes wholly within God's sovereign love.

echoes.text: For though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines; the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food; the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls: yet I will rejoice in Yahweh. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!
echoes.note: The catalogue of deprivations (failed crops, no flock) followed by 'yet I will rejoice in the LORD' parallels the list of hardships in v.35 that cannot separate from God's love, culminating in triumphant confidence (v.37).

echoes.text: If it happens, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king.
echoes.note: The three youths' confidence that 'our God whom we serve is able to deliver us' amid fire and sword resonates with believers as 'more than conquerors' through perils including 'sword' (vv.35-37).

echoes.text: But the righteous live forever, And in the Lord is their reward, And the care for them with the Most High. Therefore will they receive the crown of royal dignity And the diadem of beauty from the Lord’s hand; Because with his right hand will he cover them, And with his arm will he shield them.
echoes.note: 'The righteous live forever, and their reward is with the Lord... they will receive a glorious crown' resonates with being 'more than conquerors' and inseparable from God's love (vv.37-39).

echoes.text: And it came to pass that seven kindred also with their mother were at the king’s command taken and shamefully handled with scourges and cords, to compel them to taste of the abominable swine’s flesh. But one of them made himself the spokesman and said, What would you ask and learn of us? for we are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of our fathers. And the king fell into a rage, and commanded to heat pans and caldrons: and when these forthwith […]
echoes.note: The martyr-mother and seven sons, killed 'all day long' for covenant faithfulness yet confident of resurrection, resonate with 'for your sake we are killed all day long' read as triumphant martyrdom (vv.36-37).

echoes.text: He will deliver you in six troubles; yes, in seven no evil shall touch you. In famine he will redeem you from death; in war, from the power of the sword. You shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, neither shall you be afraid of destruction when it comes. At destruction and famine you shall laugh, neither shall you be afraid of the animals of the earth.
echoes.note: 'In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword' enumerates perils paralleling v.35's famine, sword, and danger, with God's protection through them.

echoes.text: in the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it; and it shall produce boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all birds of every wing; in the shade of its branches shall they dwell.
echoes.note: The planted sprig becomes a noble cedar 'and birds of every kind will nest in it, in the shade of its branches' — the closest verbal source for 'the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches'; a Kingdom-tree sheltering the nations.

echoes.text: The leaves of it were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all: the animals of the field had shadow under it, and the birds of the sky lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.
echoes.note: Nebuchadnezzar's great tree under which the beasts find shade and 'the birds of the air dwelt in its branches' (cf. 4:21) — a world-empire tree image transposed to the Kingdom of Heaven.

echoes.text: All the birds of the sky made their nests in its boughs; and under its branches all the animals of the field gave birth to their young; and all great nations lived under its shadow.
echoes.note: Assyria as a towering cedar in whose boughs 'all the birds of the air made their nests' — reinforces the prophetic tree-of-empire-sheltering-birds motif.

echoes.text: The birds of the sky nest by them. They sing among the branches.
echoes.note: 'Beside them the birds of the heavens dwell; they sing among the branches' — birds nesting in branches as an image of creational shelter.

echoes.text: Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah, and said, “Quickly prepare three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes.”
echoes.note: Abraham tells Sarah to take 'three measures (seahs) of fine flour' and make cakes for the divine visitors — the specific 'three measures of meal' is a distinctive verbal echo, a generous/hospitality-scaled quantity now hiding the Kingdom's leaven.

echoes.text: Gideon went in, and prepared a young goat, and unleavened cakes of an ephah of meal. He put the meat in a basket and he put the broth in a pot, and brought it out to him under the oak, and presented it.
echoes.note: Gideon prepares an ephah of flour (roughly three seahs) for the angelic visitor — another theophany-meal of this large measure.

echoes.text: When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, with three bulls, and one ephah of meal, and a bottle of wine, and brought him to Yahweh’s house in Shiloh. The child was young.
echoes.note: Hannah brings an ephah of flour to the house of the LORD — large-measure meal in a sacred context; faint.

echoes.text: They are all adulterers. They are burning like an oven that the baker stops stirring, from the kneading of the dough, until it is leavened.
echoes.note: The leaven left to rise by the baker; one of the few OT uses of leavening as a process working through dough, here neutral-to-positive rather than the usual negative valence.

doctrine.title: Nicene Creed
doctrine.article: the Holy Spirit, the giver of life

doctrine.title: Nicene Creed
doctrine.article: the life of the world to come

notes.text: Truth — In the true worship of God, in the profession, belief, practice and defense of the true religion. So truth here contains all duties to God, as righteousness doth his duties to men, and uprightness the right manner of performing both sorts of duties. With thee - That is, in thy judgment, to whom he often appealed as the witness of his integrity.

Child — So he was in years: not above twenty years old; and withal (which he principally intends) he was raw and unexperienced, as a child, in state affairs. Go out, &c. - To govern my people, and manage affairs.

In the midst — Is set over them to rule and guide them. A metaphor from the overseer of divers workmen, who usually is in the midst of them, that he may the better observe how each of them discharges his office. Chosen - Thy peculiar people, whom thou takest special care of, and therefore wilt expect a more punctual account of my government of them.

An understanding heart — Whereby I may both clearly discern, and faithfully perform all the parts of my duty: for both these are spoken of in scripture, as the effects of a good understanding; and he that lives in the neglect of his duties, or the practice of wickedness, is called a fool, and one void of understanding. Discern - Namely in causes and controversies among my people; that I may not through mistake, or prejudice, or passion, give wrong sentences, and call evil good, or good evil. Absalom, that was a fool, wished himself a judge: Solomon, that was a wise man, trembles at the undertaking. The more knowing and considerate men are, the more jealous they are of themselves.
Wonderful — In regard of the deep mysteries, the most excellent directions, and the exceeding great and precious promises of God contained in them.
Panted — I thirst after thy precepts, and pursue them eagerly.
Steps — My motions and actions.
Rivers — Plentiful tears, witness of my deep sorrow for God's dishonour, and for the miseries which sinners bring upon themselves.

Likewise the Spirit — Nay, not only the universe, not only the children of God, but the Spirit of God also himself, as it were, groaneth, while he helpeth our infirmities, or weaknesses. Our understandings are weak, particularly in the things of God our desires are weak; our prayers are weak. We know not - Many times. What we should pray for - Much less are we able to pray for it as we ought: but the Spirit maketh intercession for us - In our hearts, even as Christ does in heaven. With groanings - The matter of which is from ourselves, but the Spirit forms them; and they are frequently inexpressible, even by the faithful themselves.

But he who searcheth the hearts — Wherein the Spirit dwells and intercedes. Knoweth - Though man cannot utter it. What is the mind of the Spirit, for he maketh intercession for the saints - Who are near to God. According to God - According to his will, as is worthy of God. and acceptable to him.

And we know — This in general; though we do not always know particularly what to pray for. That all things - Ease or pain, poverty or riches, and the ten thousand changes of life. Work together for good - Strongly and sweetly for spiritual and eternal good. To them that are called according to his purpose - His gracious design of saving a lost world by the death of his Son. This is a new proposition. St. Paul, being about to recapitulate the whole blessing contained in justification, (termed "glorification," ver. 30,) first goes back to the purpose or decree of God, which is frequently mentioned in holy writ. To explain this (nearly in the words of an eminent writer) a little more at large:-When a man has a work of time and importance before him, he pauses, consults, and contrives; and when he has laid a plan, resolves or decrees to proceed accordingly. Having observed this in ourselves, we are ready to apply it to God also; and he, in condescension to us has applied it to himself. The works of providence and redemption are vast and stupendous, and therefore we are apt to conceive of God as deliberating and consulting on them, and then decreeing to act according to "the counsel of his own will;" as if, long before the world was made, he had been concerting measures both as to the making and governing of it, and had then writ down his decrees, which altered not, any more than the laws of the Medes and Persians. Whereas, to take this consulting and decreeing in a literal sense, would be the same absurdity as to ascribe a real human body and human passions to the ever-blessed God. This is only a popular representation of his infallible knowledge and unchangeable wisdom; that is, he does all things as wisely as a man can possibly do, after the deepest consultation, and as steadily pursues the most proper method as one can do who has laid a scheme beforehand. But then, though the effects be such as would argue consultation and consequent decrees in man, yet what need of a moment's consultation in Him who sees all things at one view? Nor had God any more occasion to pause and deliberate, and lay down rules for his own conduct from all eternity, than he has now. What was there any fear of his mistaking afterwards, if he had not beforehand prepared decrees, to direct him what he was to do? Will any man say, he was wiser before the creation than since? or had he then more leisure, that he should take that opportunity to settle his affairs, and make rules (or himself, from which he was never to vary? He has doubtless the same wisdom and all other perfections at this day which he had from eternity; and is now as capable of making decrees, or rather has no more occasion for them now than formerly: his understanding being always equally clear and bright, his wisdom equally infallible.

Whom he foreknew, he also predestinated conformable to the image of his Son — Here the apostle declares who those are whom he foreknew and predestinated to glory; namely, those who are conformable to the image of his Son. This is the mark of those who are foreknown and will be glorified, 2 Tim. ii, 19. Phil. iii, 10, 21.

Them he — In due time. Called - By his gospel and his Spirit. And whom he called - When obedient to the heavenly calling, Acts xxvi, 19. He also justified - Forgave and accepted. And whom he justified - Provided they "continued in his goodness," chap. xi, 22, he in the end glorified - St. Paul does not affirm, either here or in any other part of his writings, that precisely the same number of men are called, justified, and glorified. He does not deny that a believer may fall away and be cut off between his special calling and his glorification, chap. xi, 22. Neither does he deny that many are called who never are justified. He only affirms that this is the method whereby God leads us step by step toward heaven. He glorified - He speaks as one looking back from the goal, upon the race of faith. Indeed grace, as it is glory begun, is both an earnest and a foretaste of eternal glory.

What shall we say then to these things — Related in the third, fifth, and eighth chapters? As if he had said, We cannot go, think, or wish anything farther. If God be for us - Here follow four periods, one general and three particular. Each begins with glorying in the grace of God, which is followed by a question suitable to it, challenging all opponents to all which, "I am persuaded," &c., is a general answer. The general period is, If God be for us, who can be against us? The first particular period, relating to the past time, is, He that spared not his own Son, how shall he not freely give us all things? The second, relating to the present, is, It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? The third, relating to the future, is, It is Christ that died - Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?

He that — This period contains four sentences: He spared not his own Son; therefore he will freely give us all things. He delivered him up for us all; therefore, none can lay anything to our charge. Freely - For all that follows justification is a free gift also. All things - Needful or profitable for us.

God's elect — The above-cited author observes, that long before the coming of Christ the heathen world revolted from the true God, and were therefore reprobated, or rejected. But the nation of the Jews were chosen to be the people of God, and were therefore styled, "the children" or "sons of God," Deut. xiv, 1; "holy people," Deut. vii, 6; xiv, 2; "a chosen seed," Deut. iv, 37; "the elect," Isaiah xli, 8, 9; xliii, 10; "the called of God," Isaiah xlviii, 12. And these titles were given to all the nation of Israel, including both good and bad. Now the gospel having the most strict connection with the Books of the Old Testament, where these phrases frequently occur; and our Lord and his apostles being native Jews, and beginning to preach in the land of Israel, the language in which they preached would of course abound with the phrases of the Jewish nation. And hence it is easy to see why such of them as would not receive him were styled reprobated. For they no longer continued to be the people of God; whereas this and those other honourable titles were continued to all such Jews as embraced Christianity. And the same appellations which once belonged to the Jewish nation were now given to the gentile Christians also together with which they were invested with all the privileges of "the chosen people of God;" and nothing could cut them off from these but their own wilful apostasy. It does not appear that even good men were ever termed God's elect till above two thousand years from the creation. God's electing or choosing the nation of Israel, and separating them from the other nations, who were sunk in idolatry and all wickedness, gave the first occasion to this sort of language. And as the separating the Christians from the Jews was a like event, no wonder it was expressed in like words and phrases only with this difference, the term elect was of old applied to all the members of the visible church; whereas in the New Testament it is applied only to the members of the invisible.

Yea rather, that is risen — Our faith should not stop at his death, but be exercised farther on his resurrection, kingdom, second coming. Who maketh intercession for us - Presenting there his obedience, his sufferings, his prayers, and our prayers sanctified through him.

Who shall separate us from the love of Christ — Toward us? Shall affliction or distress - He proceeds in order, from less troubles to greater: can any of these separate us from his protection in it; and, if he sees good, deliverance from it?
All the day — That is, every day, continually. We are accounted - By our enemies; by ourselves. Psalm xliv, 22.
We more than conquer — We are not only no losers, but abundant gainers, by all these trials. This period seems to describe the full assurance of hope.

I am persuaded — This is inferred from the thirty-fourth verse, in an admirable order: - Neither death" shall hurt us; For "Christ is dead:" "Nor life;" 'is risen" Nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers; nor things pre- sent, nor things to come;" "is at the right hand of God:" "Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature;" "maketh intercession for us." Neither death - Terrible as it is to natural men; a violent death in particular, ver. 36. Nor life - With all the affliction and distress it can bring, ver. 35; or a long, easy life; or all living men. Nor angels - Whether good (if it were possible they should attempt it) or bad, with all their wisdom and strength. Nor principalities, nor powers - Not even those of the highest rank, or the most eminent power. Nor things present - Which may befall us during our pilgrimage; or the whole world, till it passeth away. Nor things to come - Which may occur either when our time on earth is past, or when time itself is at an end, as the final judgment, the general conflagration, the everlasting fire. Nor height, nor depth - The former sentence respected the differences of times; this, the differences of places. How many great and various things are contained in these words, we do not, need not, cannot know yet. The height - In St. Paul's sublime style, is put for heaven. The depth - For the great abyss: that is, neither the heights, I will not say of walls, mountains, seas, but, of heaven itself, can move us; nor the abyss itself, the very thought of which might astonish the boldest creature. Nor any creature - Nothing beneath the Almighty; visible enemies he does not even deign to name. Shall be able - Either by force, ver. 35; or by any legal claim, ver. 33, &c. To separate us from the love of God in Christ - Which will surely save, protect, deliver us who believe in, and through, and from, them all. In this chapter St. Paul, after strongly declaring his love and esteem for them, sets himself to answer the grand objection of his countrymen; namely, that the rejection of the Jews and reception of the gentiles was contrary to the word of God. That he had not here the least thought of personal election or reprobation is manifest,

glossa.text:
*Unutterable.* For how should that be uttered which is desired, when it is unknown? Yet it is not altogether unknown. For if it were utterly unknown, it would not be desired. And again, if it were seen, it would not be sought with groanings.

*He searcheth. ((AMBR.))* Not as though seeking what he knows not, to whom nothing is hidden, and to whom the prayer of all spirits is known.

*But we know that to them that love,* etc. As if he should say: Not only does the Holy Spirit do this, but he also makes all things turn out unto good for them that love him, whether prosperous or adverse; for such a God comforts by prosperous things, exercises by adverse. Profitable therefore are the evils which the faithful piously endure, either for the amending or the taking away of sins, or for the exercising and proving of justice, or for the showing forth of the misery of this life. For although the death of the flesh came originally from the sin of the first man, yet the good use of it has made most glorious martyrs. And therefore not only it, but all the evils of the world also, had to remain when sins were remitted, that man might have wherewith to contend for the truth, and whence the virtue of the faithful might be exercised.

*According to the purpose.* As if he should say: That they are called is from nothing else than from the predestination of God. And thence it is that *all things work together unto good:* not from merit.

*For whom,* God, *he predestinated,* that is, prepared by grace bestowed that they should believe the word of preaching: those *he foreknew,* that is, long before knew beforehand, *to be made conformable to the Son,* who is the image of the Father, in every way the same with the Father. Whence it is said: *He that seeth me seeth the Father also ((Joan. XIV))*.

*Of the image.* That we may bear the image of the heavenly, as we have borne the image of the earthly. Or *the firstborn.* Because before every creature he was not made but born, and because he was the first born without sin, and the first to rise again impassible, in which he has brethren.

*He called.* The outward calling is made through preachers and is common to the good and to the bad. But the inward is of the elect only. Of the outward it is said: *Many are called, but few chosen.* By calling predestination is fulfilled. To call is to help the knowledge concerning faith, or to prick him whom he makes to hear, and this is of the elect only. *He magnified.* This of the foreknown, not of the others, who, although they believe for a time and seem good, yet because they do not abide, are not magnified. *He magnified,* or *he shall magnify:* but this is to come, and yet it is spoken as past: because God is said to have done the things which from eternity he disposed to do; whence Isaias: *Who hath made the things that are to come ((Isa. XLIV))*. To such all things are unto good, even that they go astray, that thereby they may be the more wary, and not trusting in themselves. Four things are here mentioned: predestination, calling, justification, magnification. One is in God, and three in us. For our predestination is not in us, but hidden with him in his foreknowledge. But the three remaining are in us.

*If God be for us. ((AUG.))* God is for us, that he should predestinate us before we were, that he should call us when we were turned away, that he should justify us when we were sinners, and glorify us when we were mortal.

*He delivered up.* This is said because the Father delivered up the Son; but the author of this cup is also he himself who drinks it. Whence the Apostle: *Christ loved us, and delivered himself up for us ((Ephes. V))*. If therefore the Father delivered up the Son, and the Son himself, what did Judas do? The Father in delivering up the Son did well; the Son in delivering up himself did well; Judas in delivering up his master for avarice did ill. For that which has been bestowed upon us out of the passion of Christ shall not be reckoned to the malice of Judas; he shall have the wage of malice, Christ the praise of grace. *All things.* It is less to give us all things than for our sake to deliver Christ up to death. And so all the higher things, namely God the Trinity, are ours for the seeing and the enjoying. Things equal, namely the angels, to whom we shall be made equal in the time to come, for the living together; but now we are inferior. Things lower also are ours for the ruling. And likewise certain higher things too, as the sublime angels and all the heavenly ministries of God, are ours, not by dominion, but by use; as the things of a lord are the servants', for sustenance, namely, or ornament, or aught else of this kind.

*At the right hand of God.* In the honour wherein he is God, whose petition cannot be contemned. *He maketh intercession.* While daily he offers to the Father's countenance the man whom he assumed, and the grievous kind of death which he bore for us.
*Who shall separate us,* etc. ((CYPR.)) None of these things can separate believers, etc., *as far as* that we also may suffer for his sake: *But in all these things we overcome.*
*Neither angels, nor princes, nor virtues.* These orders are taken of the evil angels, and of the good if it might be done.

*Neither height, nor depth.* That is, neither prosperity nor adversity, whence Solomon: *Riches and poverty give me not: lest, being filled, I become a liar, or, being poor, I rob, and forswear the name of God ((Prov. XXX))*. Many sin through height, many through need. Against this Ahaz is set forth in Isaias, who would not ask a sign either in the height or in the depth. The remedy is from Christ, who was neither lifted up by the power whereby he is equal to the Father, nor troubled at the casting out of death, who is a sign in the height and in the depth: lest he should either be exalted by royal power, or troubled by hardship, as it then was on account of the war of the Assyrians.

notes.text: He proposed to them another parable — The former parables relate chiefly to unfruitful hearers; these that follow, to those who bear good fruit. The kingdom of heaven - Both the Gospel dispensation, and the inward kingdom. Mark iv, 30; Luke xiii, 18.

The least — That is, one of the least: a way of speaking extremely common among the Jews. It becometh a tree - In those countries it grows exceeding large and high. So will the Christian doctrine spread in the world, and the life of Christ in the soul.
Three measures — This was the quantity which they usually baked at once: till the whole was leavened - Thus will the Gospel leaven the world and grace the Christian. Luke xiii, 20.

glossa.text: *The kingdom is like,* etc. The kingdom of heaven is the preaching of the Gospel, concerning which elsewhere: *The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you, and shall be given to a nation bringing forth the fruit thereof ((Matth. XXI))*. Or the knowledge of the Scriptures. *To a grain of mustard seed.* It is compared to a grain of mustard seed for the fervour of faith, because it is said to drive out poisons, that is, all the doctrines of depravity. In the grain of mustard seed the humility of the Lord's incarnation may be understood. Which being received, a man put it in his garden, because Joseph, receiving the body of the crucified Saviour, buried it in a garden. It spread out branches in which the birds of the air shall rest, because he scattered preachers throughout the world, in whose words and consolations the faithful might take breath from the weariness of this life.

*But when it is grown up.* In the whole world, or in the mind of each: because no one is perfect on a sudden. It grew and became a tree, because he rose again and ascended into heaven. Or it shall have grown, that is, it shall have become known to the minds of men how great its power is. The rest appear as herbs, which grow quickly and fall: not living, but withered: that becomes not an herb, but a tree, where there are leaves with fruit, and in its diverse meanings spiritual men rest.

*Than herbs, and becometh a tree.* That is, than the doctrines of the philosophers, which grow quickly and fall, promising nothing that has life.

*In three measures of meal.* That spirit, soul and body, brought into one, may not disagree among themselves. Or the three powers of the soul are brought into one, that in reason we may possess prudence, in anger the hatred of vices, in desire the longing for virtues. Or, the woman, the Church, mixes the faith of men in three measures of meal, in the belief of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. And when it has been leavened into one, it leads us not to a threefold God, but to the knowledge of one deity, because the nature is not diverse in the several persons.

*Until it was leavened.* So long ought charity, hidden in the mind, to grow, until it change the whole mind into its own perfection, so that it love or think upon nothing beside God, which is begun here, and perfected in the other life.
